candidates.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
candidates.body: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073 . It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc). candidates.title: Visual Harness Scales General VLMs to Medical Images
candidates.body: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce \ours, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With \ours, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, \ours improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3\% to 98.3\%), renal search (57.5\% to 71.2\%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0\% to 28.2\%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with \ours. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8\% to 69.2\% with \ours, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.

(ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.

candidates.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
candidates.body: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

candidates.title: Cross-correlating the SPHEREx extragalactic background light with CMB lensing I: theoretical predictions and forecasts
candidates.body: The near-infrared extragalactic background light (EBL), which SPHEREx maps in 102 spectral channels, holds the emission lines of galaxies on top of a much brighter continuum from the integrated galaxy light (IGL) and the intrahalo light (IHL). Cross-correlating these maps with the lensing of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) isolates the emission that traces the matter, unbiased by uncorrelated foregrounds. The lines face two obstacles. Filtering along the line of sight removes the long radial modes that carry the cross-correlation, and the extragalactic continuum, a signal in its own right, is a correlated foreground for the lines. We forecast the detectability of all EBL components, in a common halo-model framework, for the SPHEREx deep fields and all-sky survey with lensing maps at the sensitivity level of Planck and the Simons Observatory (SO). Without filtering, and with all amplitudes fitted jointly, the cross-correlation with Planck lensing detects the IGL at $9σ$ in the deep fields, but not the lines. In the all-sky survey, it measures the IGL and IHL amplitudes to $1.0\%$ and $3\%$ and detects the five lines, fitted as one template, at $4.6σ$. With SO lensing, these become $0.6\%$, $1.6\%$ and $7.4σ$. In these joint fits, a filter removing radial modes longer than about $600$ Mpc costs every component $90\%$ or more of its signal-to-noise ratio, so the lines are reached by fitting the continuum, not by filtering it. These values assume a known spectral shape of the continuum. Calibrating it with the continuum's auto-spectra keeps the lines at $7.3$--$7.4σ$; fitting it from the cross-spectrum alone leaves $1.4$--$2.3σ$. The line detections vary by a factor of seven to eleven across line models. The cross-correlation is thus a robust probe of the IGL and a viable route to the emission lines, provided the continuum is modeled across the channels.

candidates.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
candidates.body: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

candidates.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
candidates.body: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

candidates.title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
candidates.body: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

candidates.title: EPI-SST: Renewal-Structured State-Space Transformers for Epidemic Forecasting
candidates.body: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.

candidates.title: WL-Headset Law: Projecting Future Headset Evolution from a Decade of Display and Mass Data
candidates.body: Tracking a decade of headset display and mass changes can inform forecasts. However, comparing headset resolution requires pixels per degree (PPD), which is often unreported and estimated using unclear assumptions. Therefore, we compile the open-source, evidence-linked HMD Resolution and Mass Database (HRMD) with 241 configurations from 2016--2026 and introduce structure- and axis-aware robust calibration (SARC) to estimate missing central PPD. Compared with official PPD, SARC reduces PPD estimation error from 14.8% for traditional geometric estimation to 3.2%. Based on HRMD, we introduce the Weight-Linked Headset Law (WL-Headset Law), which models PPD by year, mass, and category. The law reveals 7.4% annual PPD growth at fixed mass and category. Meanwhile, head-worn mass fell by 6.5% annually after category adjustment. At an eyeglass-like mass of 30g, the law projects average central PPD of 60 (normal visual acuity) around 2035 and 120 (higher acuity) around 2044 if trends persist.

candidates.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
candidates.body: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

candidates.title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
candidates.body: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.

candidates.title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
candidates.body: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.

candidates.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
candidates.body: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

candidates.title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
candidates.body: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

candidates.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
candidates.body: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

candidates.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
candidates.body: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

candidates.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
candidates.body: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.
